svg.aria-label: The Phoenician, Hebrew and Greek alphabets: the same shapes, order, names and numbers
svg.text: Same shapes. Same order. Same names. Same numbers.
The Greek letter names ARE the Hebrew letter names, and in Hebrew they are ordinary words — ox, house, camel, door, water, eye, head, tooth.
In Greek the same names mean nothing but the letters themselves.
Joseph Yahuda argued in Hebrew Is Greek (1982) that the two languages are one. This is the part of his case that is simply the consensus, which is why it goes first.
מלך — Greek says this root’s three letters by their Hebrew names: kap, lāmed, mēm.

svg.text: Υ υ · Φ φ · Χ χ · Ψ ψ · Ω ω — the five Greek added at the end, after tāw, and went on numbering from there.
The Phoenician letters above are drawn from their stroke forms, c. 9th century BC. The number column gives the value each sign carries as a numeral.
Drawn above, letter by letter. Greek turned some of them, because Phoenician runs right to left and Greek settled on
left to right. The rest it simply kept.
Twenty-two signs in one sequence, ʾālep to tāw and alpha to tau.
ἄλφα is ʾālep. βῆτα is bēt. γάμμα is gīmel. The Greek names are the Hebrew names with a Greek ending stuck on.
Ox, house, camel, door, water, eye, head, tooth. In Greek the same names mean nothing at all — a Greek child reciting
the alphabet is reciting Semitic nouns.
Both alphabets count as well as spell, 1 to 400, in the same order. Greek retired wāw, ṣādē and qōp as letters and went
on counting with them: digamma is still 6, koppa 90, sampi 900.
AND THEIR OWN HISTORIAN SAYS SO
“The Phoenicians who came with Cadmus brought into Greece, upon their settling in the land, letters which, as it seems to me, the
Greeks did not have before. The Ionians who were taught letters by the Phoenicians changed the shape of a few of them, and in using
them called them Phoenician letters — as was only right, since the Phoenicians had brought them in.”
Noted here rather than hidden, because a figure that buries it is the weaker figure: Willemijn Waal has argued that Herodotus misread his own tradition and that
Cadmus was a Greek hero, and four of the twenty-two name meanings are not securely known. The derivation itself is not in dispute — every early Greek local alphabet
comes from a Phoenician source, and the Greeks said so themselves.
the three letters of מלך — kap, lāmed, mēm · kappa, lambda, mu
Greek stopped writing it and went on counting with it
